Seventh grade science · Unit 7.9

Adaptation & Earth's History

Earth is 4.5 billion years old, and its rocks keep a diary written in layers and fossils. In Unit 5: Plate Tectonics and Rocks and Unit 8: Classifying Life you met rocks and living things; now we read the history in them, and see how traits that help survival can spread. Use Unit 0: How Science Works: this is the science of evidence from the past, where we cannot run the experiment again.

Where we left off: Unit 5 introduced rocks and plate tectonics, Unit 8 showed how living things are classified, and Unit 7.6 showed how ecosystems change. You may already have learned that rocks form in layers. Now we use layers and fossils to read Earth's history and see how traits become more common in a population.

Concept 1 · Traits that help

Adaptations match organisms to their homes

An adaptation is a trait (a body part or behavior) that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment. Individuals with helpful traits leave more offspring, so the trait becomes more common over many generations.

Analogy

The right tool for the job

A hammer, a screwdriver, and a wrench each fit one job. A cactus's thick stem and a polar bear's fat are tools tuned to a specific place.

Concept 2 · Relative dating

Reading the layers: older below, younger above

In undisturbed layers, the law of superposition says the oldest layer is on the bottom. Cross-cutting features (a dike, a fault) are younger than what they cut. This gives relative age (older or younger), not a date.

Analogy

A stack of laundry

The shirt on the bottom was put there first. A hand dug through the pile later is younger than the shirts it cut through.

Try it

Order the layers

Data

Rules of relative dating

RuleMeaning
SuperpositionBottom layers are older
Original horizontalityLayers form flat; tilted ones were moved later
Cross-cuttingA feature that cuts through is younger
InclusionsPieces inside a rock are older than the rock

Concept 3 · Radioactive clocks

Half-lives give numbers in years

Some atoms are radioactive and decay at a steady rate. A half-life is the time for half of them to decay. Measuring how much is left tells us the absolute age of a rock or fossil. Half-life is probabilistic: for a single atom, decay is a chance event and you cannot say when it will happen, but for huge numbers of atoms the overall pattern is very predictable.

Analogy

A melting ice cube

Imagine a cube that loses half of what is left every hour. After 1 hour: ½. After 2: ¼. After 3: ⅛. Measure what remains and you can tell how long it has been melting.

Try it

IsotopeHalf-lifeDates

Concept 4 · Evidence of past life

Fossils show who lived when

Fossils are preserved remains or traces of ancient life. Index fossils lived for a short time over a wide area, so finding one in a layer dates the layer. Fossils also show environments (marine fossils on land mean an ancient sea).

Analogy

Time-stamped photos

A photo with a flip phone in it was taken in the 2000s. An index fossil is the same kind of clue for a rock layer.

Try it

What does it tell us?

Real world

How fossils form

StepEvent
1An organism dies and is buried quickly
2Soft parts rot; hard parts stay
3Minerals replace or fill the hard parts
4Uplift and erosion expose the fossil

Concept 5 · Deep time

Earth's history on a clock

Earth is about 4.6 billion years old. If all that time were one day, humans would appear in the last few seconds. Major changes in life and climate are recorded in the rocks.

Analogy

The 24-hour Earth

Midnight: Earth forms. Around 4 a.m.: first life. Around 9 p.m.: first animals. Just before midnight: modern humans... and everything in recorded history fits in the last blink.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

A geologist finds a layer with trilobite fossils below a layer with fern fossils, and a granite dike cutting through both. Put the three in order from oldest to youngest and explain how you know.

Show a model answer

Trilobite layer (oldest, bottom), fern layer (above it), granite dike (youngest, because it cuts through both). Superposition gives the layer order and the cross-cutting rule gives the dike's age.

0 of 6 correct

Words to know

adaptation
A trait that helps survival and reproduction.
natural selection
Individuals with helpful traits leave more offspring.
fossil
Preserved remains or traces of ancient life.
index fossil
Short-lived, widespread fossil that dates layers.
superposition
Older layers lie below younger ones.
relative age
Older or younger, not a number.
absolute age
Age in years.
half-life
Time for half of a radioactive sample to decay.
stratum
A rock layer.
extinction
Disappearance of a species.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $8): layered play dough or sand/colored gravel in a clear jar, a deck of 20 cards of Earth events, real or replica fossils, 100 pennies/candy for half-life, string for a 4.6 m timeline.

  • Concept 1: Layer colored sand in a jar, then cut a "fault" and sequence the events.
  • Concept 2: Half-life with candy: shake and remove marked pieces, graph the remaining.
  • Concept 3: Lay out a 4.6-meter string timeline with 1 mm = 1 million years.
  • Concept 4: Make a fossil from clay and a shell, then explain each step.
  • Concept 5: Play a predator–prey camouflage game with colored paper dots on patterned cloth.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Animals choose to adapt." Traits vary and selection acts over generations.
  • "Fossils are always bones." Trace fossils (tracks) count.
  • "Humans lived with dinosaurs." They are separated by ~65 million years.
  • "Half-life means half the time." It is the time for half the atoms to decay.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions. Method link: stress that we cannot repeat history, so scientists use multiple independent lines of evidence (Unit 0): rocks, fossils, and radioactive dating that agree.
